pairs.rationale: Both ascribe prophetic communication to God. Hebrews says God spoke long ago to the fathers in prophets in many portions and ways; Peter says human beings spoke from God, borne along by the Holy Spirit rather than human will. The timing, means and Spirit detail are not treated as identical wording.

Both describe creative agency through the figure being discussed. Hebrews says God made the ages through the Son whom He appointed heir; Colossians says all things were created in, through and for Him. Ages is not silently replaced with all things, and the distinct in/through/for and heir clauses remain.

Upholding all things by the word of His power corresponds to all things holding together in Him. Colossians also says He is before all things; Hebrews adds radiance, imprint, purification and enthronement. The sustaining descriptions are compared without importing every additional claim into the other unit.

Both connect exalted status with the name bestowed or inherited. Philippians says God highly exalted Him and gave the name above every name; Hebrews compares His inherited name with theirs in describing superiority to angels. The granted/inherited and every-name/angels formulations remain distinct, without supplying an unprinted name here.

The first son-and-today-begotten saying closely matches the Lord's decree in Psalm2:7. The Psalm's appointed-king context says son in its own printed case and pronouns; Hebrews applies the saying in the Son-versus-angels question. No particular begetting date or an explicit Jesus name is added to the Psalm.

The Father-to-him and Son-to-Me promise closely corresponds to Samuel's father/son promise in a house-and-throne context. Samuel continues with correction if wrongdoing comes; Hebrews quotes the shorter relationship promise in its angel contrast. That unquoted wrongdoing clause is not assigned to Jesus.

The call for all His angels to bow down in the Psalm corresponds to all God's angels worshiping the firstborn here. The Psalm also rebukes carved-image worship; Hebrews frames the saying through bringing the firstborn into the inhabited world. That setting and again wording are not dated or added to the Psalm.

The makes-His-angels and ministers-as-fire formula closely corresponds to the Psalm. The supplied Psalm says angels winds and ministers a burning fire; Hebrews says angels spirits and ministers a flame of fire. Winds and spirits remain as actually translated rather than silently normalized.

The throne address to God, enduring-age language and upright royal rod or scepter correspond closely to Psalm44:7. Hebrews explicitly introduces the address as concerning the Son and says scepter where the Psalm says rod. Their age-of-age and age-upon-age wording and original pronouns remain intact.

The loved-righteousness/hated-lawlessness sequence and God-your-God anointing with oil of exultation beyond companions closely match Psalm44:8. Hebrews continues its quoted address concerning the Son; the Psalm's accompanying royal garment and palace setting is not inserted into the unit.

The beginning, Lord, earth's foundation and heavens-as-handworks statement closely corresponds to Psalm101:26. Hebrews introduces it within its Son-and-angels argument; the Psalm's surrounding plea about the speaker's days is not added to that quoted creation statement.

The perishing creation, remaining addressee and garment-aging contrast closely match Psalm101:27. That Psalm unit also continues into changing the cloak; Hebrews' unit ends at growing old and continues its quotation in1:12. The original unit boundaries are retained.

The cloak/garment change and unchanged addressee with unfailing years correspond to Psalm101:27–28. Hebrews says roll them up and adds like a garment before changed; the Psalm says change them like a cloak. The close quotation retains that actual roll/change difference.

The sit-at-My-right-hand and enemies-as-footstool saying closely matches Psalm109:1. The Psalm introduces the Lord speaking to my lord; Hebrews asks to which angel such speech was ever addressed. That argumentative application is not represented as a question already printed in the Psalm.

The Psalm gives a specific angel-service description: God commands His angels to guard the addressed person and lift him on their hands. Hebrews describes ministering spirits sent for the sake of salvation's heirs. Guarding in one's ways and the broader service-for-heirs statement remain distinct, without turning physical protection into an identical full salvation claim.
